planting.note: Set rooted stem cuttings or rhizome divisions in spring into fast-draining, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; seed germination is notoriously unreliable without fire cues.

directions: Yerba santa is a drought-adapted evergreen shrub native to the dry chaparral and foothill slopes of California and southern Oregon, where it forms colonies from spreading underground rhizomes. Establish new plantings from rooted stem cuttings or transplanted rhizome divisions set into fast-draining, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun, since the resinous, sticky, lance-shaped leaves and seed have a notoriously low, fire-cued germination rate in cultivation. Once established, the deep root system needs little to no summer irrigation and resents heavy clay or regular watering, which promotes root rot. Harvest mature leaves any time after the second year; it has a long history of use brewed into a bittersweet tea for coughs and colds, and the dried leaf was historically used to mask the bitterness of other medicines.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Root semi-ripe cuttings taken in late summer and set young plants out in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, sheltered from hard freezes.

directions: Boldo is a slow-growing, aromatic evergreen shrub native to the Mediterranean-climate scrublands of central Chile, where its thick, leathery, sandpapery leaves release a strong camphor-eucalyptus fragrance when crushed. Propagate from semi-ripe cuttings taken in late summer, since seed is slow and erratic to germinate, and set young plants in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade with protection from hard freezes. Established plants tolerate heat and drought well but need winter protection or container culture outside zone 9, and in the ground it takes several years to reach a size worth harvesting. The dried leaves, rich in the alkaloid boldine, are steeped as a traditional after-meal digestive tea throughout Chile and are also used to flavor some South American liqueurs.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; do not cover deeply as germination is fastest near the surface.

directions: Tribulus is a low, trailing warm-season plant native to dry, sandy, disturbed ground across Africa, southern Europe, and Asia, grown commercially for its spiny, star-shaped fruit capsules (gokshura in Ayurveda, bai ji li in Chinese medicine) rather than its foliage. Direct sow after the soil has warmed into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; small yellow flowers appear within weeks and are quickly followed by the hard, thorny seed capsules that give the plant its common name puncture vine. Harvest capsules as they dry and turn tan, before they fully harden and disperse, since mature spines are sharp enough to puncture bicycle tires and bare feet — contain plantings to a dedicated bed, as the species self-sows aggressively and is classified as a noxious weed in parts of the western United States. Grow as a warm-season annual in most gardens; it persists as a short-lived perennial only in essentially frost-free zones.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Cold-stratify or scarify seed and direct sow in early spring into lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; germination is slow and uneven, so sow generously.

directions: Bupleurum chinense is an upright, clump-forming perennial in the carrot family grown in traditional Chinese medicine gardens for its slender taproot, known as chai hu, one of the most frequently prescribed herbs in Chinese herbal formulas. Direct sow scarified or cold-stratified seed in early spring into lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; germination is slow and uneven, so overseed generously and be patient. The narrow, willow-like leaves and small yellow umbel flowers resemble a fine-textured fennel or dill and make an attractive, airy addition to an herb border while the root develops below ground. Roots are traditionally left undisturbed for two to three growing seasons before being dug in autumn, cleaned, and dried for use in tea and decoction.

planting.note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before direct sowing in spring into deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: Chinese licorice is a rhizomatous perennial legume native to the steppes of northern China, Mongolia, and Siberia, cultivated for its sweet, fibrous root, known as gan cao, one of the most frequently used herbs in traditional Chinese medicine formulas, prized for harmonizing other herbs in a blend. Nick or soak the hard seed coat before direct sowing in spring into deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; as a nitrogen-fixing legume it tolerates poor, sandy soils but struggles in heavy, waterlogged clay. The plant spreads steadily by underground rhizomes and can become assertive in loose soil over time, so give it room or a root barrier in smaller gardens. Roots are traditionally left in the ground for three to four years to bulk up before being dug in autumn, then sliced and dried; this species is distinct from the Mediterranean licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra) more commonly grown in Western herb gardens.
